summary: This document describes how signaling intermediaries, often called Session Border Controllers, behave when performing Hosted NAT Traversal for real-time media. It covers media relaying and latching, which let devices behind NATs communicate. It is non-normative.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7362 explains how a server in the middle of a call helps two devices that sit behind different network address translators, or NATs, reach each other. The server hands out its own addresses, then sends the call back to whichever address the first media packets came from. The document is a description, not a specification, and it says plainly that this method has security weaknesses that make it unsuitable for general use on the Internet.

questions: what is a session border controller
subtitle: How a signalling intermediary finds the real address of a phone behind a NAT, and why that method is risky.

tldr.problem: SIP and similar protocols put private addresses and ports into their session descriptions, and a NAT will not let packets in until the device behind it has sent some out, so two devices behind different NATs cannot reach each other directly.
tldr.mechanism: A signalling intermediary such as a Session Border Controller rewrites the addresses so that both parties point at a media relay it controls, then watches the first media packets that arrive and sends the return traffic back to the address and port they came from. This is called latching, and it is one part of Hosted NAT Traversal.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7362 describes the mechanism so that the industry has a common name for it, and warns that latching has real security problems. The IETF advises against using it over the Internet and recommends ICE and TURN instead.

today: RFC 7362 is an Informational RFC published in September 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a description of practice rather than a specification, and its advice stands on its own: the document recommends ICE and TURN for new work.

sections.title: What Hosted NAT Traversal Is
sections.content:
The document uses the term NAT for any device that maps an IPv4 or IPv6 address and transport port number to another IPv4 or IPv6 address and port number, which covers consumer NATs, firewalls with NAT, address family translators and carrier-grade NATs. The Session Initiation Protocol and other signalling protocols that try to use a more direct path for media than for signalling are difficult to use across NATs.

Mechanisms such as STUN, TURN and ICE did not exist when SIP was first deployed, and the early versions of STUN were unreliable and suffered the problems typical of unilateral self-address fixing. For that reason, the Session Border Controllers already deployed in SIP domains began using proprietary mechanisms to let devices behind NATs talk to each other across the NATs. These mechanisms are often transparent to the endpoints and rely on a dynamic address and port discovery technique called latching. The behaviour is usually called Hosted NAT Traversal, sometimes Far-end NAT Traversal or NAT assist. The systems that perform it are frequently SBCs, though media gateways and media proxies do the same job.

The document says that a large majority of SIP domains use this approach, and that the deployment levels make its complete extinction unlikely in the foreseeable future, although it does not discuss the reasons why it is used. Its purpose is to describe the mechanisms used at the session description and media layers so that their implications and limits are understood, and to give the community a common terminology and a reference. It does not argue for the mechanism or present it as better than alternatives. Because of the security issues, latching is considered inappropriate for general use on the Internet unless those issues are solved, and the IETF advises the use of ICE and TURN instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Before ICE, TURN and STUN existed, the servers that handle SIP calls had to invent their own way of getting two phones behind different NATs talking. The method they settled on is now called Hosted NAT Traversal, and the address discovery part of it is called latching. The document describes it so that the industry has one name for it, and it recommends against using it on the open Internet.

sections.title: Why NATs Break Signaling and Media
sections.content:
Three problems stand in the way of NAT traversal for protocols such as SIP. First, the addresses and port numbers that a NATed user agent puts into the session description body, or its equivalent, are not usable across the Internet, because they are the private addresses of that user agent rather than the addresses and ports the NAT will map them to. Second, the policies built into NATs and made explicit in firewalls mean that packets from outside the NAT cannot reach the user agent until the user agent has sent packets out first. Third, some NATs apply endpoint-dependent filtering to incoming packets, so a user agent may only be able to receive packets from the same remote address and port that it sends packets to.

To overcome these problems, a signalling intermediary on the public side of the NAT performs Hosted NAT Traversal for both signalling and media. In the typical deployment the media relay and the signalling intermediary are co-located and share one IP address, and the relay address is usually in the same address family as the signalling, so both travel over IPv4 or both over IPv6. The port numbers the intermediary introduces are typically allocated dynamically, and the allocation strategy is entirely implementation dependent and often differs from one product to the next.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things go wrong. The phone puts its own private address in the call setup, and the other side cannot use it. The router will not pass an incoming call through to the phone until the phone has made an outgoing call. And some routers only let the phone receive from the exact address and port the phone has already written to, which rules out a peer it has not spoken to yet.

sections.title: Impact on Signaling
sections.content:
Along with codec and other media information, session establishment signalling carries addressing information that may be private and not globally routable, so the intermediary modifies it and gives each peer the public addressing information of a media relay it controls. Once an offer has been sent, the generator of the offer has to be ready to receive media on the addresses and ports it advertised, but in practice the media may or may not arrive, depending on the implementations in the session, on local policies and on the call scenario.

Two examples are given. If a session description offer came from a user agent behind a NAT, the intermediary cannot send media to it until an answer has been given and latching has occurred. And when the intermediary sends an offer in an INVITE to a residential customer's user agent and receives a session description back in a provisional response, the intermediary may decide on policy grounds not to send media to that customer until the final response arrives, for example to prevent toll fraud.
sections.plainLanguage: The server rewrites the addresses in the call setup so that both phones are told to send their audio to the server's relay. That rewrite also means the phone on the other side has to be ready to receive media on the address it advertised, even though the server may decide on policy not to send anything until the call is answered.

sections.title: How Latching Works
sections.content:
A user agent behind a NAT streams media from an address and port that are only valid inside its own network, and once the packets cross the NAT that tuple is mapped to a public one. The user agent usually does not know the public mapping and advertises the private one, so during setup the intermediary does not yet know the addresses the two parties will really use. Media relays therefore latch.

The mechanism works in steps. After receiving an offer from Alice, the intermediary allocates a set of address and port tuples on its media relay and advertises them to Bob, so that Bob sends all his media toward Alice to those tuples. After receiving Bob's answer, the intermediary allocates a second set of tuples and replaces Bob's address in its answer to Alice, so Alice sends her media to the second set. The relay then receives media on the allocated ports and uses the source address and port of each arriving packet as the destination for media going the other way; that is the latching. When Alice's media arrives on the second tuple, its source address is the public interface of Alice's NAT, so anything the relay sends back there reaches Alice. Bob's source address is latched in the same way for the other direction.

Latching is normally done once per peer and is not allowed to change until a new offer and answer are exchanged, for example in a later call or after a peer has been on hold. The reason is security: once a session has started, a user agent is not expected to start streaming from a different port without sending a new offer first, and a change may indicate an attempt to hijack the session. A port change can also come from a re-mapping in a NAT between the intermediary and the user agent, so more advanced intermediaries allow some flexibility while weighing the security consequences. Some intermediaries apply extra logic before latching, to avoid latching onto a previous media sender, which the industry calls rogue RTP.

For latching to work, the user agent behind the NAT needs symmetric RTP, meaning it uses the same ports for sending as for listening, and it must be able to start sending media without waiting to receive first. Media relays need to begin receiving before they start sending, which creates a risk of deadlock when both ends of a session are connected to different intermediaries that both provide Hosted NAT Traversal. To prevent it, relays often start streaming toward the addresses in the offer and answer before any inbound traffic arrives.

Many intermediaries support latching only over UDP, and some also support it over TCP. TCP latching is more complicated: the user agent behind the NAT must be made the TCP client, sending the initial SYN packet to the intermediary. If both user agents of a TCP media session are behind NATs, the intermediaries typically force both to be the TCP clients and splice the two TCP connections together. Two caveats are raised by participants. The first is that the user agents are not aware that latching happens, which makes the mechanism impossible to combine with ICE, because overwriting address information in offers and answers can trigger the ICE mismatch rules and stop ICE working altogether. The second is that media goes through a relay rather than directly over the IP-routed path, which reduces scalability and adds latency but also lets the operator see that media is flowing, judge its quality and learn why it failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The server watches which address and port the first audio packets come from, and sends the return audio to that address. It then stops listening for new addresses until the call is renegotiated, because a change of address mid-call could be someone trying to steal the call. The phone has to use the same port to send and receive, and it has to speak first, or the two sides can wait for each other forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concern is that an intermediary may latch onto an incorrect and possibly malicious source. ICE provides authentication tokens, carried in its ice-ufrag and ice-pwd attributes, that confirm a peer's identity before media exchange begins. Without such authentication, a malicious source could try a resource exhaustion attack by flooding all the possible media-latching UDP ports on the intermediary so that calls fail. Intermediaries have mechanisms to prevent this and to alert an administrator, but a sufficiently sophisticated attacker may bypass them for a while. The most common example is restricted latching, where the intermediary will not latch onto packets from any source address other than the one the user agent uses for signalling, so it simply ignores the attacker's packets. The restriction may be loosened to allow media from a range of addresses on the same network, to support decomposed user agents and third-party call control, but such configurations are usually made case by case because relaxing the rule widens the attack surface.

These problems remain if the attacker knows the public source address of the user agent that is really making the call, because the attacker can then flood the intermediary's addresses and ports with packets spoofing that address, though the effect is limited to media from that address rather than to every call. A malicious source could also send media to a latching port in the hope of being latched onto. Restricted latching helps here too, because the intermediary has not seen the matching signalling and will not latch. An issue remains if the attacker is in the IP routing path and can spoof the real user agent's address, or if the attacker is behind the same NAT as the legitimate user agent, in which case its packets will be latched onto and the media will go to the attacker. That case is of particular concern with carrier-grade NATs, where many devices sit behind one address; the legitimate call would end when a person hangs up, but an automated participant such as an answering machine might not hang up. The attacker could also forward the media to the real user agent, in which case the attack would probably go undetected and succeed.

Secure RTP would mitigate these threats and, with the right key negotiation, protects the media from being monitored in transit, so it should be used independently of Hosted NAT Traversal. If the intermediary that latches takes part in the SRTP key exchange, it can simply refuse to latch onto a source it cannot authenticate; failing to implement and use SRTP is a serious threat to users behind carrier-grade NATs and is considered a harmful practice.

Two further effects follow from the intermediary having to modify the session description. The user agent cannot use S/MIME, and cannot sign a request or verify a received one with the SIP Identity mechanism, unless the intermediary re-signs it; neither of those is widely deployed, so this is not a concern at present. On privacy, relaying media is sometimes seen as a way of hiding one's IP address from the other party, but that is no longer an advantage held by Hosted NAT Traversal alone, since a client can obtain the same effect from a relay it controls itself, such as TURN.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has no way to check that the packets arriving on its relay port really come from the phone it is talking to, so an attacker can try to be mistaken for the phone. Restricting the server to latch only onto the address the phone used for signalling blocks most of this, but an attacker sharing a NAT with the phone, as happens behind a carrier-grade NAT, can still win. The document says encrypted media should be used on top, and that the server should refuse to latch onto anything it cannot authenticate.

viz.caption: THE WAYS LATCHING CAN BE ABUSED

items.title: Latching on the wrong source
items.text: The relay takes the first address it sees, which may not be the phone it is expecting.

items.title: Flooding the relay ports
items.text: Sending to every latching port tries to exhaust the intermediary so that calls fail.

items.title: Spoofing the phone's address
items.text: If the attacker knows the public address, it can send packets that look like the real phone.

items.title: Sharing the NAT
items.text: An attacker behind the same carrier-grade NAT is latched onto in place of the real phone.

items.title: Forwarding the media on
items.text: An attacker that relays the media to the real phone makes the attack hard to notice.
